I have spoken to people in my own constituency who have never asked anyone for help before and who now find themselves counting coins at the till and putting items back. That is the reality behind the figures we trade across this Chamber.

The response cannot simply be to wait and hope that the pressure eases of its own accord. Wages in large parts of the country have barely moved in real terms for over a decade, and the buffer that families once had has been worn away by successive shocks. When prices rise five per cent and incomes rise by one, the arithmetic is brutal and it falls entirely on the household. For a family on a low income, food and energy are not a small share of the budget that can be squeezed; they are most of the budget.

So I would ask the Minister to look seriously at three things. First, uprating benefits properly and in time, rather than with a lag that guarantees a real-terms cut precisely when the pressure is greatest. Second, targeted support on energy bills for those on the lowest incomes, delivered automatically rather than through schemes people have to discover and apply for. Third, a genuine plan on housing costs, because rents in many of our towns are now rising faster than anything else in the basket and no amount of tinkering elsewhere will offset that.

Inflation is often discussed as a technical matter for the Bank and the Treasury. For the people I represent it is not technical at all. It is the difference between coping and not coping, and we should legislate and budget with that in front of us.

That is precisely why the guidance accompanying the regime matters as much as the statutory text itself. Authorities will want to know, in practical terms, what compliance looks like: what records they are expected to keep, at what point in the decision-making process the duty bites, and how they should evidence that they have properly considered the matters set out in the clause. If we leave those questions to be resolved case by case in the courts, we will have imposed a cost on the very bodies we are asking to deliver, and we will have delayed the benefit to the people the regime is designed to help.

I can tell the House that the guidance is being developed in consultation with the representative bodies, and that we intend to publish it in draft before commencement so that there is a proper opportunity for comment. That is not a courtesy; it is a practical necessity. The people who administer these decisions day to day will spot the operational difficulties that none of us in this Chamber will anticipate.

On the question of monitoring, I understand the concern that a duty without oversight can drift into a formality. The Department will collect and publish data on how the duty is being applied, and I would expect the relevant committee to take an interest in those returns. Where there is evidence of systematic failure, we will act, and we have the power to issue further directions.

I would say gently to Members who have argued for a heavier enforcement mechanism at the outset that there is a balance to be struck. A regime that begins in an adversarial posture tends to produce defensive compliance rather than good practice. I would rather start with clarity and support, hold the power in reserve, and be judged on whether beneficiaries actually receive what they are entitled to. That is the test I am content to be measured against.

It was drafted for a world of paper files and formal registries, and it is being applied to a world of instant messaging, shared drives and records that are created and deleted at a scale nobody envisaged when it was passed.

I would say this to Members on all sides, because I do not think this is a party matter. Every one of us relies on the civil service to implement what we legislate. It was about whether the business could afford to lose a day's trading, and the person carrying the consequence of that decision was the employee standing at a bus stop in dangerous conditions with no service running.

I have heard from workers in retail, in hospitality and in contract cleaning who were told in plain terms that if they did not come in they would not be paid, and in some cases that they should not bother coming back. These are not workers with the leverage to argue. Many are on hours that vary week to week, and the threat of being rostered down is a real one. A request to employers is worth very little to somebody in that position.

So my question to the Minister is straightforward. When the next red alert is issued, and there will be a next one, what protection will exist for a worker who makes the safe decision? Will there be a clear statement, with legal force behind it, that no employee should suffer detriment for not travelling during a red alert? Will there be any mechanism for the Workplace Relations Commission to deal with such cases quickly, rather than months later when the employment has already ended?

I accept that these events are difficult to plan for and that the emergency response overall was handled well by the services involved. I am not making a criticism of them. But we cannot keep relying on the good sense of employers as though it were uniformly distributed. Most are decent. The ones who are not are precisely the ones whose workers most need the State to speak clearly on their behalf, and at the moment it does not.

I want to put some of that in concrete terms, because the abstractions get us nowhere. A woman came to my clinic last week with two children. She has worked in the same job for eleven years. Her rent went up by an amount she cannot meet, she was served notice, and she has been looking for four months. She has viewed properties where forty people queued on the street. She is not asking for charity. She is asking why a person in full-time employment cannot secure a roof for her family in the country where she was born and where she pays her taxes.

The Government's answer, repeated in every debate, is that supply is the issue and supply takes time. Supply is an issue, and I do not pretend that a housing system can be turned around in a quarter. But the choice about who bears the cost of the delay is a political choice, made here, and it is being made against tenants at every turn. We could act on rent increases. We could end no-fault evictions properly rather than with a list of exemptions wide enough to drive a lorry through. We could resource local authorities to buy where tenants are being sold out from under them. Each of those is available now and each has been declined.

So when Ministers tell us that they are doing everything they can, I would ask them to be precise about what they mean. They are doing everything they are willing to do. Those are different statements, and the families I have described understand the difference better than anyone in this Chamber.

The industry has had a considerable period in which to demonstrate that self-regulation works, and the evidence before the Committee suggests that progress has been real but uneven. Some of the larger platforms have invested substantially and can now remove flagged material within hours. Others, including some with very significant reach, take days, and a few appear to treat the process as a public relations exercise rather than an operational responsibility.

The difficulty with voluntary arrangements is that they reward the diligent and cost the negligent nothing. A company that spends heavily on moderation is at a competitive disadvantage to one that does not, and there is no mechanism to correct that. That is a classic case for regulation, and it is the argument I would put to those colleagues who are instinctively reluctant to legislate in this area. Regulation here does not restrain the responsible; it removes the advantage currently enjoyed by the irresponsible.

I would add two cautions. First, speed of removal is a useful measure but it is not the only one, and if we legislate on that metric alone we will get over-removal, with lawful speech caught up in automated systems tuned to avoid penalties. Any framework needs to include a proper route of appeal for material taken down in error, and that route has to be usable by an ordinary person rather than only by someone with a lawyer.

Second, we should be honest that the worst material is often hosted well beyond our jurisdiction. Legislation here will not solve that on its own, and it will require sustained work with other Governments and with the international bodies that coordinate takedown requests.

None of that is an argument for delay. It is an argument for getting the design right. I hope the Government will bring forward proposals in this session, and I hope they will publish them in draft so that the Committee can do its work properly.

What I am asking for is not complicated. First, engagement between the Office of Public Works, the Department and the insurance sector to establish what exactly is driving these quotations, because the operators themselves cannot get a straight answer. Second, consideration of whether the State can assist with a guarantee or a group scheme, as has been done in other sectors where the market has effectively withdrawn. dogs are killed for their meat every year, many of them stolen family pets, many of them transported for days in conditions that would be criminal if the animal were a farm animal in this country. The cruelty involved is not incidental to the trade; it is built into it, because the animals are moved live, in bulk, over long distances, by people with no interest in their welfare.

Members may reasonably ask why we need legislation here when the practice is not, so far as anyone knows, occurring in this country. There are two answers. The first is that while the slaughter of a dog for human consumption is already caught by our animal welfare law, the consumption itself is not an offence, and neither is possessing or importing the meat. That is a gap. It is a small gap, but it is a real one, and it means that we cannot say, straightforwardly, that this trade has no place here.

The second answer is about our standing to argue the case elsewhere. When our diplomats and our welfare organisations press other Governments to act, the first response is very often to ask what our own law says. Closing this gap costs us nothing and removes that objection entirely. Several other countries have already legislated on precisely this basis.

I want to be careful about one thing. This Bill is not, and must not become, a vehicle for lecturing other cultures. There are campaigners in the countries most affected who are doing braver work than any of us, often at real personal cost, and they have asked for support rather than condemnation. The Bill is drafted narrowly. It creates an offence, it defines it clearly, and it does nothing else.

I hope the House will give it a fair wind, and I commend the motion to the House.

They apply to what happens in this country as much as to what we fund overseas, and they cut across health, education, housing, transport and the environment. No single Department can compel action across that range, and the Department that leads on overseas development is not structured to do so domestically.

Our Committee's view, reached after hearing from a wide range of witnesses, is that the coordinating function needs to sit at the centre of Government, with the authority that comes from that. In the countries where implementation has gone furthest, that is precisely the model that has been adopted. Where responsibility has been parked in a single sectoral Department, reporting tends to become a compilation exercise: each Department sends in a description of what it was doing anyway, the descriptions are stapled together, and the result tells us very little about whether outcomes are actually improving.

That matters for the credibility of the review itself. Other countries read these documents. Our development partners read them. If ours reads as a public relations exercise, we lose some of the moral authority we bring to the international discussions where we have genuinely led.

I would also press the Secretary of State on the involvement of the devolved administrations and of local government. A great deal of the delivery on these goals happens at council level, and the Committee heard from several authorities that have adopted the framework enthusiastically with no support at all from the centre.

Finally, on scrutiny: whichever Department leads, there should be a commitment to lay the review before Parliament and to allow a debate on it in Government time. A report that cannot be questioned in this Chamber is not really a report to anyone. I hope the Secretary of State can give us that commitment today.

The pattern that emerges from the cases they have highlighted is depressingly consistent. Money leaves a country where it was stolen or extorted, passes through a chain of companies in jurisdictions where ownership is opaque, and arrives here to be parked in property. The property sits, often empty, appreciating. Nobody is prosecuted. The person from whom the money was ultimately taken has no realistic remedy, and frequently no idea where their national wealth went.

We have passed legislation on this. We have registers, we have unexplained wealth orders, and we have sanctions regimes. What we have not had is enforcement at anything like the scale of the problem. The agencies responsible are asked to take on litigants with effectively unlimited resources, in cases that take years, with budgets that would not cover a mid-sized commercial law firm's annual costs. When an agency loses one such case and faces an adverse costs order that consumes a significant share of its budget, the rational institutional response is to bring fewer cases. That is exactly what we have seen.

So my central ask of the Minister is about resourcing and about costs protection. Give the enforcement agencies a budget proportionate to the sums at stake, and give them protection against ruinous costs where they act reasonably and lose. Those two changes would do more than another round of legislation.

I would add one further point. The professional services that facilitate this, the lawyers, the accountants, the company formation agents and the estate agents, are almost never held to account. Until there is real consequence for the enablers, the flow will continue, and we will be back in this Chamber having this debate again in three years' time.

The purpose of the change is to bring our practice into line with how the House actually functions, rather than with how it functioned when the standing orders were first drafted. In practice, the call for the yeas and nays has become a formality that consumes time without serving any scrutiny function, and every member in this place knows it.

I want to address the concern that has been raised about the rights of individual members and of members who do not belong to a recognized party. That concern is legitimate and it should be answered rather than dismissed. As drafted, the provision allows a single representative of a recognized party to request a recorded vote. It does not extend that right to an independent member, and I accept that this is a real change in the position of those members. My view is that the accompanying provision, which permits five members rising together to secure a recorded division, preserves the essential protection. Others disagree, and I think the committee should look at whether the threshold is set correctly.

The broader point is about the use of this Chamber's time. We spend a considerable number of hours each session on procedural votes whose outcome nobody doubts. Those hours come out of debate, out of committee work and out of the time members spend in their constituencies. Reform that recovers that time is worth having, provided it does not quietly remove the ability of a minority to force the House to declare itself.

That is the balance we are trying to strike, and I do not claim we have struck it perfectly. This is a proposal, it is before the House, and I would genuinely welcome amendment. What I would resist is the suggestion that any change to these standing orders is by definition an attack on the rights of the opposition. Some changes are simply overdue housekeeping.

A class opened without a teacher who has the relevant training, and without a special needs assistant who has been given more than a day's introduction, is not provision. It is a room. Parents can tell the difference within a fortnight, and so can the children.

At the moment the training pathways are fragmented. A teacher who wants to specialise has to find a course, often at their own expense, frequently in their own time, and sometimes at a considerable distance from where they live and work. Some do it anyway, and I want to acknowledge them, because the system currently depends on the goodwill of people who go looking for qualifications nobody is offering them. That is not a workforce plan.

What I would like to see is straightforward in principle. A recognised postgraduate qualification, funded or substantially subsidised, available part-time and remotely, with protected release time from the school. Alongside that, a proper induction for special needs assistants, who currently receive very little and who are often the adults spending the most hours with the child. And a career structure, so that a teacher who develops this expertise is not effectively choosing to step off the promotional ladder.

I would also say something about continuity. Children in these settings are particularly affected by staff turnover, and turnover is high precisely because the roles are demanding and the support is thin. Investment in training is wasted if the trained person leaves within two years.

We are, as I said, all learning here. But we have been learning for a long time now, and the families waiting for places are entitled to ask when the learning turns into a plan with dates and numbers attached. I would ask the Minister to indicate when we might see one.

That means sustaining the broadcasting services that still reach Russian audiences, and funding them properly rather than treating them as a residual line in a budget. It means keeping open the visa routes for journalists, academics and dissidents who need to leave, and doing so quickly, because a route that takes eight months is not a route for someone under surveillance. I would ask the Minister specifically about students. There are Russian students in this country who have spoken out and who cannot go home. Their funding arrangements have in some cases collapsed along with the banking links. What provision is being made for them? These are precisely the people who will matter in whatever comes after Putin, and how we treat them now will be remembered.

I would also ask about the cultural and academic links that have been severed. Some of that was unavoidable and some of it, frankly, has been performative. Cancelling a long-dead composer punishes nobody in Moscow. Maintaining contact with Russian scientists who oppose the war costs us very little and preserves something we will need later.

To spend the weekend rightly celebrating the importance of players' mental wellbeing, and then to have this arrangement come to light within days, does look to many people like a considerable distance between what is said and what is done. I do not think that impression is unfair.

The Government's position is that where an organisation takes on commercial partnerships, it accepts a degree of responsibility for how those partnerships sit alongside its stated values. That is not a legal obligation and I am not proposing to make it one this afternoon. It is a matter of judgment, and the judgment here appears to have been made badly. I would encourage the governing body to look again at it, and I would say that the reaction of supporters over the last few days ought to weigh heavily in that reconsideration.

On the wider question that the hon. Member has been pursuing, we are looking at the regulatory framework and I expect to be able to say more before the summer. There are real questions about advertising, about the exposure of young supporters, and about the relationship between sport and sectors whose products carry known harms. Those questions are being examined properly rather than in response to a single weekend's headlines, but the events of that weekend certainly do not slow the work down.

I would finish by paying tribute to the campaign itself. Heads Together and the organisations working alongside it have shifted something genuine in this country. Men who would never have discussed their mental health a decade ago now do so, and sport has been a large part of why. That achievement deserves better protection than it has received, and I will convey that view directly when I meet the governing body next month. I am happy to update the hon. The State's position was that the works fell within the original scope. The court found substantially for the contractor. That is the sequence, and I set it out plainly because it is the pattern we see again and again.

What troubles me is not that a project came in over budget. Construction is uncertain and any honest assessment accepts that some overrun is inevitable on a complex build. What troubles me is the structure of the incentive. A contractor bidding for public work knows that the lowest tender wins, and knows equally that variations after award are where the margin is recovered. So the tender is priced to win, not to build. Everybody in the industry understands this. Everybody in the relevant Departments understands it too. And yet we continue to award on the same basis and then express surprise at the same outcome.

I would ask the witnesses two things. First, what analysis has been done across the capital programme on the gap between tender price and final account? Not case by case, but in aggregate, because if that gap is systematically twenty or twenty-five per cent then our published capital budgets are not really budgets at all.

Second, what is the position on the design work? A significant proportion of these variations trace back to designs that were incomplete at the point of tender. If we tendered from finished designs, we would pay more up front and considerably less overall. Has that been costed?

I would also like to know whether anyone was held responsible on the State's side for the conduct of that litigation, which was itself expensive and which, on the court's findings, was not well founded. I have not seen any indication that anybody was.

Competition policy works with a lag. A merger blocked today prevents a price increase in three years that nobody will ever be able to point to, which makes this the least politically rewarding file in government and one of the more important ones.

Madeleine arrived in my riding as a young woman with very little, and she built something remarkable. She nursed in the local hospital through the years when staffing was thin and equipment was scarce, and she was known on her ward for staying past the end of her shift because a patient had nobody else sitting with them. Colleagues have told me that she remembered the names of the families as well as the patients, and that she wrote letters, in her own hand, to people who had been discharged months earlier simply to ask how they were getting on.

When she retired she did not stop. She organized the meal program at her parish, she drove neighbours to appointments in the city, and she sat on the board of the community health centre for eleven years, where she was, by every account I have heard, the most persistent and least easily discouraged person in the room. She raised money for equipment. She lobbied three levels of government, including my own office, with a directness that I came to look forward to.

She was also a fierce defender of French-language services in a region where those services are not always easy to obtain. She insisted that a patient should be able to describe their pain in the language they think in, and she was right about that, and she said so until people listened.

Madeleine passed away last month surrounded by her children and grandchildren. On behalf of everyone she looked after, and everyone she badgered into doing better, I offer my condolences to her family and my gratitude for a life spent, exactly as she said, doing what needed to be done.

I would say two things about how that door is kept open. The first is that it requires channels that survive periods of maximum tension, which means maintaining diplomatic contact even when doing so is politically uncomfortable here. Our embassy presence, the work done through third parties, and the technical discussions between officials that never make a headline are the mechanisms by which a crisis is de-escalated at three in the morning. There is a difference between a warming world that is harder to live in and a warming world that has crossed a threshold beyond which the trajectory is no longer ours to influence, and everything we do in this decade determines which of those we are dealing with.

That distinction should shape how we think about adaptation, and at the moment it does not. A certain amount of change is now locked in regardless of emissions decisions taken from here, and the people who will bear it first are, as always, those with the least capacity to absorb it.

In concrete terms for this country, that means flood defence for communities that have already flooded three times in a decade, and an honest conversation with a small number of communities about whether defence is viable at all. It means water infrastructure built for a rainfall pattern we no longer have. It means a health service prepared for heat events that were once considered exceptional. It means agriculture supported through transitions in what can be grown where.

None of that reduces the obligation to cut emissions, and I want to be emphatic about that, because adaptation is sometimes deployed as an argument for delay by people who have no intention of adapting either. The two are not alternatives. Every tonne we do not emit reduces the adaptation burden on somebody, usually somebody poorer and further away.

What I am asking for is that the adaptation plan be published with costings and with statutory review, on the same footing as the mitigation plan, rather than as an annex.

For most of our membership we were a net recipient. On the specific matter before us, I support the Government's position and I want to say why in plain terms. Where international humanitarian law is breached, we should say so, and we should say so regardless of who the perpetrator is. The value of a principle lies entirely in its application to cases where applying it is inconvenient. A country that condemns violations by its adversaries and finds nuance when its friends are involved has not adopted a principle; it has adopted a tactic, and everybody can see the difference.

The first point I would make is about the workforce. When we discuss the transition, we discuss it largely in terms of megawatts and targets and dates. The people I worked alongside are welders, electricians, subsea engineers, control room operators and helicopter crews.
